passages.section: The algebraic PCP theorem: a detailed account of the Lean proof
passages.quote: A polynomial-time verifier can check membership in any NP language by reading a constant number of bits from a suitably encoded proof. It uses only logarithmically many random bits, accepts a correct proof with certainty, and rejects every purported proof of a false statement with probability at least one half. We reconstruct the algebraic argument in Troy Lee's Lean formalization and explain how its implementation and machine-simulation theorems establish these resource bounds.

passages.section: Correcting an outer value at a prescribed point
passages.quote: Fix a target $a\in F^k$. A point oracle $f$ has degree-one labels, and an auxiliary table is supplied for each line through $a$. Choose a uniform direction $v\in F^k$, a nonzero uniform parameter $z\in F^\times$, a uniform homogeneous label $L$, an inner correction direction, and an independent inner-test seed. Run the inner test on the line's auxiliary row. If it fails, reject. Otherwise correct that row at $\Phi(z)$ and compare with $f(a+zv,L)$. If the comparison fails, reject. If both checks pass, return the correction at $\Phi(0)$, with the same inner correction direction and label.

passages.section: From every NP verifier to a graph
passages.quote: Represent a computation by $T(n)+1$ rows of bounded configurations, with the witness length and bits included. The constraints enforce the initial row, every adjacent transition and the accepting final row. Halting is padded by the machine's bounded-evaluation convention. Every true computation gives such a tableau within the space bound. Conversely, determinism and the transition constraints force each successive row to be the actual machine configuration, so an accepting tableau gives a witness with $R(x,w)=1$.

passages.section: From every NP verifier to a graph
passages.quote: A constraint over an alphabet of size $A$ is converted to Boolean constraints by one-hot coding. Each source variable receives $A$ bits, exactly one of which is true; its true index is the encoded symbol. Validity constraints enforce this condition. A relation inspects the relevant one-hot blocks and accepts precisely the tuples accepted by the original finite relation. The alphabet size and local arity are constants fixed by the original machine. [The finite-domain encoding][lean-one-hot] proves that decoding a satisfying one-hot assignment and encoding a source assignment preserve all constraints.

passages.section: From every NP verifier to a graph
passages.quote: To encode NAE by a graph, make a palette triangle with colours $0,1,2$. Each Boolean variable has two adjacent vertices, one for itself and one for its negation; both are joined to palette vertex 2. They must therefore receive complementary colours 0 and 1. Constant literals 0 and 1 use the corresponding palette vertices. For a NAE clause, make a new triangle and join its $i$-th vertex to the vertex for its $i$-th literal. If the three literal colours are equal, every vertex of the new triangle is forbidden that colour, so three distinct colours are impossible. If the literals are not all equal, the triangle can be coloured: for literal colours $(0,0,1)$, use triangle colours $(1,2,0)$; complementing or permuting yields the other cases. A colouring of the whole graph can first be relabelled so the palette has colours 0,1,2, after which it yields a satisfying Boolean assignment. The [NAE graph theorem][lean-nae] proves these two constructions.
